items.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 establishing sustainability reporting standards for voluntary use by undertakings protected by the value chain cap
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.locator: Recital 5; Annex I, paragraphs 6(b), 7, 12 and 44 to 64 (Comprehensive Module, C1 to C9, and paragraphs 49 to 52 on Scope 3)
items.quote: Applying the Basic Module is a prerequisite for applying the Comprehensive Module.
items.why: The current text of the Comprehensive Module and the source of the quotation. Nine disclosures: C1 strategy and business model, C2 practices and policies described, C3 greenhouse gas reduction targets and climate transition, C4 climate risks, C5 further workforce characteristics, C6 human rights policies and processes, C7 human rights incidents, C8 revenues from certain activities, C9 gender diversity in the governance body. Scope 3 emissions are a 'consideration' under paragraphs 49 to 52, reported if the undertaking decides to. Recital 5 says undertakings applying the standard are not obliged to seek assurance. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office.

items.title: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2026) 500 final, accompanying the two delegated regulations of 3 July 2026
items.locator: Section 4.3.1 and section 4.3.2, text and table, PDF page 21 (printed page 20); footnote 37
items.quote: The VSME CBA was developed for a population of undertakings with up to 250 employees.
items.why: Source of the figure. Estimated cost of applying both modules together: first year EUR 8,500 to 9,500 for undertakings with fewer than 20 employees and EUR 17,500 to 22,800 for those with 20 to 250; recurring EUR 4,500 to 4,800 and EUR 8,500 to 11,000. The document says the estimates cannot be extrapolated to undertakings with 250 to 1 000 employees. Estimates for EU firms from a cost-benefit analysis of the 2024 standard, not measured UK costs.

items.title: Voluntary sustainability reporting standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME)
items.locator: Paragraphs 45 to 65 (Comprehensive Module, C1 to C9), in particular paragraphs 49 and 50 to 52
items.quote: The undertaking may indicate, if any, the most senior level of the undertaking accountable for implementing them.
items.why: The original Comprehensive Module, which templates in circulation still follow. Shows that naming a senior person accountable is optional ('may'), and that Scope 3 was already a consideration to be reported 'if the undertaking decides to provide this metric', not a numbered disclosure. A standard-setter's technical advice, superseded as the legal reference by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560.

items.title: UK SRS S2: climate-related disclosures
items.locator: Paragraph 29(a)(i) (PDF pages 14 to 15); Appendix A, defined terms 'Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions' and 'Scope 3 categories' (PDF page 22)
items.quote: Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions are categorised into these 15 categories
items.why: The UK standard that listed customers will report against. It requires Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions and defines Scope 3 by the fifteen categories of the Greenhouse Gas Protocol value-chain standard, the first of which is purchased goods and services, so a supplier's emissions are part of the customer's figure. Voluntary unless another rule requires it; an investor-focused standard, not designed for small firms.

items.title: PS26/19: Aligning listed issuers' sustainability disclosures with international standards (policy statement)
items.quote: many issuers face challenges accessing the data needed to make Scope 3 emissions disclosures
items.why: Why the hardest comprehensive request, value-chain emissions, will keep arriving. The regulator put Scope 3 on a comply-or-explain basis because listed companies struggle to get the data, and gave one year's relief. Rules apply to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. The rules bind listed companies, not their suppliers.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CB: Contents of non-financial and sustainability information statement
items.quote: an analysis of the resilience of the company’s business model and strategy, taking into consideration different climate-related scenarios
items.why: What the largest UK companies must already disclose on climate: governance, risk identification, strategy, scenario analysis, targets and indicators. The topics mirror C3 and C4 of the Comprehensive Module, which is why large UK customers and lenders ask suppliers about targets and climate risk. Subsection (2A) was inserted by S.I. 2022/31. Applies only to companies within section 414CA.

items.title: 2026 post-implementation review of the SECR regulations 2018
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.locator: 'Objective 4: Proportionate reporting burden', page 19, paragraph under Figure 3
items.quote: intensity ratios and Scope 3 data were more challenging
items.why: UK evidence on where the difficulty lies. Even among large reporting companies, Scope 3 data and intensity ratios were the hard part while core energy and Scope 1 and 2 data were easy. Supports treating value-chain emissions as estimates with a stated method. Respondents were large and quoted companies.

items.title: PPN 006: Taking account of Carbon Reduction Plans in the procurement of major government contracts
items.locator: Paragraph 11; Carbon Reduction Plan template, sections on baseline and current emissions
items.quote: a defined subset of Scope 3 emissions
items.why: A UK request that goes beyond basic data: bidders for large central government contracts must commit to net zero by 2050 for UK operations and report Scope 1, Scope 2 and a subset of Scope 3 emissions, with the plan published on their website. An example of a comprehensive-level request with an identifiable buyer.

items.title: Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard
items.publisher: Greenhouse Gas Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development)
items.locator: Chapter 5, section 5.4 'Overview of scope 3 categories', page 31 (PDF page 33); figure 5.2 and table 5.3
items.quote: This standard categorizes scope 3 emissions into 15 distinct categories
items.why: The international method that both the EU voluntary standard and UK SRS S2 point to for value-chain emissions. Sets the fifteen categories and the distinction between data from specific activities in the value chain and secondary data, which is the basis for stating an estimation method.

items.title: Supervisory statement 5/25: Enhancing banks' and insurers' approaches to managing climate-related risks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Paragraph 4.28 (printed pages 17 to 18, PDF pages 19 to 20); paragraphs 4.25 and 4.31
items.quote: the credibility of the client, counterparty, investee and policyholder's transition plan and its positioning versus competitors
items.why: Why finance asks comprehensive-level questions. The prudential regulator lists what a bank or insurer should weigh in a material client relationship: exposure to transition and physical risk, the credibility of the client's transition plan, its adaptation plans and the vulnerability of its supply chain. These map onto the targets, transition and climate-risk disclosures (C3 and C4). Supervisory expectations for banks and insurers, applied only to relationships the firm judges material; no duty on the client. Commenced 3 December 2025.

items.title: Thematic Review: Climate-related Financial Disclosures by AIM and Large Private Companies
items.locator: Section 12, 'Targets and key performance indicators', page 23; executive summary, page 4
items.quote: it was unclear whether targets were in place but not disclosed, or if there were no targets to disclose
items.why: UK regulator's findings on how well companies evidence targets, the hardest part of the comprehensive set. Even among companies legally required to disclose climate targets and performance against them, only half gave all the required information. Supports the brief's warning about a target nobody can evidence. Published 21 January 2025. A review of a selection of annual reports of AIM and large private companies in their first years of mandatory reporting, not of small suppliers; findings are qualitative.

items.title: Modern Slavery Act 2015, section 54: Transparency in supply chains etc
items.locator: s.54(1), (2), (4) and (5); turnover threshold in S.I. 2015/1833, regulation 2 (£36 million)
items.quote: its due diligence processes in relation to slavery and human trafficking in its business and supply chains
items.why: The UK binding rule behind human rights questions to suppliers. A commercial organisation supplying goods or services with total turnover of at least £36 million must publish a yearly statement of the steps taken to ensure slavery and human trafficking are not taking place in its supply chains, which is why large clients ask suppliers about policies, due diligence and incidents (C6 and C7). The duty is to publish a statement, which may say no steps were taken; it places no duty on the supplier. The page is up to date to 5 October 2026 and notes changes not yet in force.

items.title: Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights: Implementing the United Nations 'Protect, Respect and Remedy' Framework
items.publisher: United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
items.locator: Principle 14 and commentary, printed page 15 (PDF page 20); principles 15 and 16 on policy commitment and due diligence
items.quote: The responsibility of business enterprises to respect human rights applies to all enterprises regardless of their size, sector, operational context, ownership and structure.
items.why: The international standard that customers' human rights questions are drawn from. It expects every enterprise to have a policy commitment, a due diligence process and a route to remedy, while the commentary accepts that a smaller firm's processes will be simpler. Gives a small supplier the benchmark for a proportionate human rights policy and complaints route. Not legally binding; endorsed by the UN Human Rights Council in resolution 17/4 of 16 June 2011 (document HR/PUB/11/04).

items.title: Transition Plan Taskforce Disclosure Framework
items.publisher: Transition Plan Taskforce (published on the IFRS Foundation's site)
items.locator: Section 3, the five elements, page 21; Figure 3, page 15 (sub-element 3.1, engagement with value chain)
items.quote: An entity shall disclose how it is engaging with its value chain, industry peers, government, public sector, communities, and civil society
items.why: The UK framework against which a transition plan is judged credible, and so the template behind lenders' and large clients' questions on targets and transition. It shows what a full plan contains (ambition, implementation, engagement, metrics and targets, governance) and that large companies are expected to disclose how they engage suppliers. Dated October 2023. Voluntary; written for listed companies and financial firms, so a small supplier should treat it as the shape of the question, not a requirement on itself. Read on the IFRS Foundation's site, which now hosts the document.

items.title: Assurance of sustainability reporting: consultation and government response
items.quote: the government has tasked the FRC to establish an interim regime and register by mid 2026
items.why: The UK position on assurance, which the top level of this criterion depends on. Anyone may currently offer assurance of sustainability data; the government has decided on a voluntary register of providers run by the Financial Reporting Council, with legislation to follow when parliamentary time allows. So a claim of 'assured' data should name the provider and say whether it is registered. The page was last updated on 30 January 2026; whether the interim register opened on time was not checked in this pass. Policy direction, not law.

items.title: Scope 3 Emissions in the UK Reporting Landscape: Call for Evidence Analysis Report
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.quote: Though it was acknowledged that primary data is preferable, estimates are often used in lieu
items.why: UK government evidence on why value-chain emissions are estimates. Respondents reported reliance on spend-based data, inconsistent methods between organisations, double counting, and confidentiality concerns about supplier information, and said estimates can undermine comparability. Supports stating the method beside any value-chain figure. Dated May 2024. A thematic analysis of 184 self-selected consultation responses, not a survey and not policy.

items.title: Harmonizing corporate carbon footprints
items.publisher: Klaaßen and Stoll, Nature Communications 12, 6149 (Springer Nature)
items.quote: In a case study of the tech sector, we find that corporate reports omit half of the total emissions.
items.why: Peer-reviewed evidence that value-chain emissions figures are unreliable even from large, well-resourced companies: reporting was inconsistent between channels, boundaries were incomplete and activities were left out. The sector studied is technology, which makes it directly relevant to the emissions of bought-in computing and AI services. A case study of large technology companies, published in 2021; not small firms and not UK-specific. Open access on the publisher's site.

items.title: Completing the SME carbon profile: scalable prediction of scope 3 emissions
items.publisher: Phillpotts and co-authors, Journal of Industrial Ecology 30, 23-38 (Springer Nature)
items.quote: a business's Scope 3 emissions remain rarely measured and as a result are poorly understood
items.why: Peer-reviewed UK research, 2026, on value-chain emissions in small firms. Using financial transaction data for more than 150,000 UK small and medium-sized enterprises, the authors produce spend-based estimates and report that the approach predicts purchased goods and services well and narrower categories less well. Shows both that a small firm can estimate without heroic effort and that the result is a model output whose method must be stated. Spend-based estimates rest on sector averages, not the firm's own suppliers; the lead author's work was funded by Lloyds Banking Group, with which three of the authors are affiliated. Open access on the publisher's site.

items.title: Senate Bill No. 253, Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (chaptered 7 October 2023)
items.locator: Section 2, adding Health and Safety Code section 38532, subdivisions (b)(2), (b)(5) and (c)(1)
items.quote: including the use of industry average data, proxy data, and other generic data in its scope 3 emissions calculations
items.why: International comparator. California requires companies with revenues above one billion dollars that do business in the state to disclose Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions with independent assurance, and expressly allows Scope 3 to be calculated from industry averages and proxies. A second large jurisdiction where value-chain emissions are mandatory for big companies and estimates are accepted, so UK suppliers to US groups can expect the same questions. This is the bill as chaptered on 7 October 2023; later amendments and the state board's regulations, which set the reporting dates, were not read in this pass. Do not take a date from this page.
